title: Day 3 on VA ECMO: a falling saturation
subtitle: A 58-year-old man after an anterior STEMI, cannulated in the cath lab, now with discordant pulse oximetry between hand and foot.
objectives: Explain the two-pump physiology of peripheral femoro-femoral VA ECMO and predict where the mixing zone sits as native cardiac output changes.
Choose monitoring sites at cannulation that will detect differential hypoxemia before it causes harm, and state what each site does and does not tell you.
Build a differential for upper-body hypoxemia on VA ECMO that includes circuit failure, not only watershed physiology.
Rank the management options for differential hypoxemia by invasiveness and by what they do to LV afterload, and justify a sequence.
Recognize how LV unloading strategies (ECPELLA) and ECMO flow changes interact with the watershed.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 58-year-old man is in the CTICU on day 3 of peripheral VA ECMO. He had a late-presenting anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock, underwent PCI of the LAD, and was cannulated in the cath lab the same day via the right femoral vein (multistage drainage cannula, tip in the RA) and the left femoral artery (return cannula with a distal perfusion catheter). The ECMO flow has been stable. He is intubated and sedated. Vasoactive support has been weaned to a low-dose inotrope. [REVIEW]

On admission two days ago the bedside team noted that he had aspirated during the index arrest. His chest radiograph this morning shows worsening bilateral airspace opacities. Ventilator: volume control, lung-protective settings, moderate PEEP, FiO2 0.5. [REVIEW]

The overnight fellow reports the first-ever drop in pulse oximetry. The reading on the right hand has fallen into the mid-80s. The pulse oximeter on the left toe reads 100%. [REVIEW]

Before looking at any new data, consider how this patient was set up for monitoring on day 1.

questions.prompt: You are being handed this patient. Which monitoring sites and sampling points would you want established on any peripheral VA ECMO patient from the start, and what question does each one answer? Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
The organizing idea is that peripheral VA ECMO creates two circulations in one aorta: antegrade native ejection from the LV and retrograde flow from the femoral return cannula. The mixing zone (watershed) sits wherever those two pressures balance. Anything proximal to it is perfused by the lungs. Anything distal is perfused by the oxygenator. The monitoring plan exists to find the watershed and to tell the fellow which circulation is supplying the brain and the coronaries.

- **Right radial arterial line.** The brachiocephalic trunk is the first arch branch, so the right arm is the most proximal site you can sample and is the best available surrogate for the blood reaching the right carotid and, closer still, the coronaries. ELSO and most expert reviews recommend the right radial as the default arterial line site on peripheral VA ECMO for exactly this reason. [REVIEW] A left radial or a femoral line will read oxygenator blood and give false reassurance.
- **Pulse oximetry on the right hand, separately from a lower-extremity probe.** A discordant pair is the cheapest early-warning system you have.
- **Bilateral cerebral NIRS.** It is not a validated numeric target, but a widening left-right asymmetry or a trend down on the right while the left holds is a signal that the watershed has moved proximally. Rosenberg and colleagues cite bilateral cerebral oximetry as standard monitoring for this purpose. [REVIEW]
- **Post-oxygenator blood gas.** This answers a different question: is the circuit delivering what you think? A post-oxygenator PaO2 that is not in the hundreds on FiO2 1.0 means the membrane is failing, and no amount of watershed reasoning will fix that. Sampling it is also how you avoid the trap in the East-West (RIDDLER) case elsewhere in this library.
- **Echo, repeated.** Aortic valve opening, LV ejection, pulsatility on the arterial trace, and in some hands the location of the mixing zone in the aorta on TEE (Rosenberg and colleagues, citing Asija and colleagues, note the watershed can sometimes be visualized). [REVIEW]
- **Distal perfusion catheter function** is unrelated to watershed physiology but is the other reason to check the cannulated leg. Do not conflate the two.

What is not on this list: a femoral arterial line as the sole arterial access. It will look perfect until the patient has a stroke.

questions.prompt: Which arterial sampling site best reflects the oxygen content of the blood perfusing the coronary arteries and the right cerebral hemisphere on femoro-femoral VA ECMO, and why do the other candidate sites (left radial, contralateral femoral, post-oxygenator port) fail that job?
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: Right radial artery.** The brachiocephalic trunk is the most proximal arch branch. The right arm is the earliest site to fall when native output of poorly oxygenated blood reaches the arch, and it is the closest practical surrogate for the coronaries, which are more proximal still.

Why the alternatives fall short:

- **Left radial artery.** The left subclavian is the third arch branch and is more often supplied by retrograde ECMO flow as the watershed moves distally. It reads too reassuring.
- **Femoral artery on the non-cannulated side.** This samples oxygenator blood and will remain normal regardless of what the lungs are doing.
- **Post-oxygenator circuit port.** Essential for assessing circuit performance, but it tells you nothing about what the native heart is ejecting into the arch.

The coronaries arise from the sinuses of Valsalva, proximal to every arch branch. Computational modeling by Stevens and colleagues suggests myocardial hypoxia develops before cerebral hypoxia as native output rises, which means even a normal right radial gas does not fully exclude coronary hypoxemia. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
You go to the bedside. The arterial line is in the right radial artery. The arterial waveform has become clearly pulsatile over the past 12 hours where previously it was nearly flat.

Right radial ABG on ventilator FiO2 0.5: pH 7.38, PaCO2 41, PaO2 52, saturation 86%. [REVIEW]

Post-oxygenator gas on sweep FiO2 1.0: PaO2 above 400, PaCO2 36. [REVIEW]

ECMO circuit: flow unchanged from yesterday, no change in revolutions per minute, delta pressure across the oxygenator unchanged, no visible clot. [REVIEW]

Cerebral NIRS: right has drifted down over the night, left is stable. [REVIEW]

Bedside TTE: LVEF has improved from severely reduced on day 1 to moderately reduced today. The aortic valve opens with every beat. There is no new pericardial effusion. RV function is mildly reduced, unchanged. [REVIEW]

Ventilator: tidal volumes and PEEP unchanged from yesterday. Plateau pressure has risen modestly. Chest radiograph shows worse bilateral opacities. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: What is happening, mechanistically, and what have you excluded with the data above? Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is differential hypoxemia, also called North-South syndrome, Harlequin syndrome, or dual circulation. Two things happened at once: the LV recovered enough to eject with every beat (pulsatile trace, aortic valve opening, improved EF), and the lungs got worse (aspiration pneumonitis, worse radiograph, higher plateau). The native heart is now pumping poorly oxygenated blood antegrade with enough force to push the watershed distal to the brachiocephalic trunk. The right arm and right carotid territory, and almost certainly the coronaries, are being perfused by the lungs. The left toe is being perfused by the oxygenator.

What the data exclude:

- **Oxygenator failure.** Post-oxygenator PaO2 above 400 on FiO2 1.0 with an unchanged transmembrane pressure gradient says the membrane is fine. If that number had been 80, this would be a circuit problem, and the fix is a circuit change, not a cannulation change.
- **Circuit flow problem.** Flow and RPM unchanged. A sudden flow drop with chatter would point to drainage insufficiency, which has its own differential (hypovolemia, tamponade, cannula migration).
- **Sampling error.** The line is in the right radial and the NIRS asymmetry corroborates it.

What the data do not fully exclude: coronary hypoxemia. The coronaries are proximal to the right radial, so if the right radial is desaturated the coronaries are at least as bad. A rising troponin or new ischemic ECG changes should be looked for rather than assumed absent. [REVIEW]

The conceptual trap is to treat this as an ECMO problem. It is a native lung problem that ECMO cannot reach, and the native heart has become strong enough to matter.

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative:
The attending asks for your plan. The options on the table, roughly in order of invasiveness, are:

1. Optimize the native lungs: recruit, raise PEEP and FiO2, bronchoscopy for aspirated material, diuresis if volume-permissive, treat the pneumonitis.
2. Increase ECMO flow to push the watershed proximally.
3. Reduce native ejection (deeper sedation, lower inotrope) to let ECMO flow dominate.
4. Add a second return limb to the venous side (VAV configuration) so oxygenated blood reaches the right heart and lungs.
5. Move the arterial return to the right axillary or subclavian artery, or convert to central cannulation.
6. Add a transvalvular LV unloading device (ECPELLA).

The patient's hemodynamics are currently stable on the existing support.

questions.prompt: Rank the six options and name your first step. Be explicit about what the Impella option would do to the physiology.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: Optimize ventilation and treat the lung disease, then reassess, with escalation to a VAV configuration if upper-body oxygenation does not recover.** The problem is the lungs. Expert reviews (Asija and colleagues) and ELSO guidance place lung optimization first because it is reversible, non-invasive, and addresses the cause. If it fails, VAV cannulation is the most commonly recommended next step because it delivers oxygenated blood to the pulmonary circulation and therefore to whatever the LV ejects. [REVIEW]

Why the alternatives fall short:

- **Add an Impella to unload the LV and reduce the antegrade ejection of hypoxemic blood.** This gets the physiology backwards. An Impella draws blood from the LV and ejects it into the ascending aorta. If the lungs are the problem, the Impella delivers more hypoxemic blood to the coronaries and arch, worsening differential hypoxemia. Rosenberg and colleagues explicitly describe the ECPELLA configuration as a setup in which North-South physiology is seen. An Impella is a reason to be more vigilant about watershed hypoxemia, not a treatment for it. [REVIEW]
- **Increase ECMO flow until the right radial saturation normalizes.** This sometimes works, and it is tempting because it is a dial. The cost is higher LV afterload from more retrograde flow, which can worsen LV distension and pulmonary edema, which is the very problem you are trying to escape. It also assumes the drainage side can supply the extra flow. Reasonable as a temporizing move while you do other things, not as the plan.
- **Deepen sedation and stop the inotrope to suppress native ejection.** Suppressing a recovering heart to make a monitor look better is a step backwards. It may transiently help but it also delays weaning, and the LV recovery is the thing you want.

The order of operations most expert reviews converge on is: fix the lungs, then re-route oxygenated blood to the right heart (VAV), then move the arterial return proximally (axillary, or central) if VAV is inadequate or impractical. Where to draw the line between those steps is institution- and patient-specific. [NMH protocol, insert]

questions.prompt: Lung optimization over the next 12 hours produces only a modest improvement. The team decides to convert to VAV. Describe how you would configure and manage the VAV circuit, and name the two new problems you have just created.
questions.modelAnswer:
Configuration: a second return cannula is placed in the internal jugular vein (or an additional venous site) and connected to the arterial outflow via a Y-connector, so oxygenated blood from the oxygenator is split between the femoral artery and the right atrium. The venous return limb is typically fitted with a clamp or flow restrictor so the split can be adjusted. Flow through each limb must be measured separately with ultrasonic flow probes. [REVIEW]

The two new problems:

1. **Flow distribution.** The venous limb is a low-resistance path, so without restriction it steals flow from the arterial limb. You now have to balance oxygenation (more flow to the venous side) against systemic support (more flow to the arterial side), and the balance changes as the heart recovers. Each adjustment needs a re-check of right radial gas, post-oxygenator gas, and systemic perfusion markers. [REVIEW]
2. **Recirculation.** Oxygenated blood returned to the RA can be drawn straight back into the drainage cannula, especially if the two venous cannula tips are close. Recirculation shows up as a rising pre-oxygenator saturation with little improvement in the right radial gas. Cannula tip separation on imaging matters. [REVIEW]

Anticoagulation targets and the specific flow split are institution-specific. [NMH protocol, insert]

Two less obvious points. First, VAV raises the chance that the drainage cannula cannot supply total flow, so watch for chatter. Second, VAV is often a bridge: as the lungs recover, the venous limb is clamped and the patient returns to VA, or as the heart recovers, the arterial limb is removed and the patient is on VV. The fellow should be thinking about which direction this patient is heading from the day the VAV is placed.

stages.title: Complication
stages.narrative: Day 6. On VAV, right radial saturation has been acceptable for 36 hours. This morning the perfusionist notes the arterial limb flow has fallen, the venous limb flow has risen, and the mean arterial pressure has drifted down. Lactate has risen slightly. The right radial gas is fine. The LV looks better again on echo. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: What is the most likely explanation, and what is the trap in interpreting the right radial gas as reassuring here?
questions.modelAnswer:
The most likely explanation is that the venous limb is taking a progressively larger share of circuit flow, either because the restrictor has loosened, because systemic vascular resistance has changed, or because the arterial limb has partially occluded (kinking, thrombus, cannula position). The result is less systemic (arterial) support at a moment when the lungs may still be inadequate. The right radial gas is reassuring about oxygen content but not about oxygen delivery: the patient can be well oxygenated and underperfused at the same time. Falling MAP and rising lactate are the delivery signals.

Actions: re-measure both limb flows against the intended split, inspect the arterial limb and cannula, check for distal perfusion catheter issues, and recalibrate the restrictor. If the LV has recovered enough, this may be the moment to discuss stepping down to VV support rather than fighting the split. That conversation needs an echo-based assessment of whether the native heart can carry full cardiac output, which is the subject of the weaning literature rather than this case. [REVIEW]

The general lesson: on hybrid configurations, every monitor answers one narrow question. Oxygen content, flow, and perfusion need separate checks every time the patient changes.

teachingPoints:
- Peripheral VA ECMO creates two circulations in one aorta. The watershed moves distally as the native heart recovers and proximally as it fails. Nothing about the circuit numbers tells you where it is.
- The right radial artery is the most proximal practical sampling site and should be the default arterial line on peripheral VA ECMO. The coronaries are more proximal still and may be hypoxemic before the right radial falls. [REVIEW]
- Differential hypoxemia is a lung problem made visible by cardiac recovery. Confirm the circuit is working (post-oxygenator gas) before attributing hypoxemia to the watershed.
- Management sequence most reviews support: optimize the lungs, then VAV, then move the arterial return proximally or centrally. Increasing ECMO flow is a temporizing dial with an afterload cost.
- LV unloading devices that eject into the ascending aorta (Impella) can worsen differential hypoxemia when the lungs are injured. The ECPELLA patient needs the same vigilance as the recovering-heart patient.
- Hybrid circuits trade one problem for two: flow distribution and recirculation. Measure each limb, re-check after every change.
pitfalls:
- A femoral arterial line as the only arterial access. It reads oxygenator blood and will look normal while the brain is hypoxemic.
- Attributing upper-body hypoxemia to the watershed without sampling the post-oxygenator gas. Oxygenator failure looks similar at the right radial and has a completely different fix.
- Responding to differential hypoxemia by deepening sedation and dropping inotropes. This suppresses the recovery you are waiting for.
- Adding an Impella to a hypoxemic VA ECMO patient without recognizing that it delivers more native, lung-conditioned blood to the coronaries and arch.
- Treating a normal right radial gas on VAV as proof of adequate support. Content and delivery are separate questions.
- Forgetting that the venous return limb of a VAV circuit will steal flow unless restricted and measured.
controversies:
**Whether to raise ECMO flow.** Some experienced centers raise flow first because it is immediate and reversible. Others avoid it because higher retrograde flow raises LV afterload, worsens distension and pulmonary edema, and can create the very lung injury that produced the problem. There is no trial. The honest statement is that it is a reasonable temporizing step while definitive measures are arranged, and a poor long-term plan. [REVIEW]

**VAV versus upper-body arterial return.** VAV is more widely used and does not require a surgical cutdown, but introduces flow-split and recirculation management. Axillary or subclavian return (surgical graft) delivers oxygenated blood directly to the arch and avoids the split, at the cost of a procedure, hyperperfusion of the ipsilateral arm, and center-dependent expertise. Which comes first is a center preference, not an evidence-based ordering. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Oxygen saturation targets for the upper body.** There is no validated right radial saturation threshold that defines harm. Clinicians act on trend, NIRS asymmetry, and downstream markers. Any numeric trigger written into this case is institutional practice, not guideline. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Whether coronary hypoxemia should change decisions independently of cerebral hypoxemia.** Modeling suggests the coronaries fall first. Whether this should lower the threshold for reconfiguration in a patient with an acceptable right radial gas but rising troponin is unsettled. [REVIEW]
discussWithAttending: At what point would you accept worse native lung protection (higher PEEP, higher FiO2, recruitment) to delay a VAV conversion, and what would make you stop accepting it?
In this patient the LV is recovering. Would you ever deliberately slow that recovery (less inotrope, more sedation) to keep the watershed distal? Under what circumstances, if any?
Your center's default for refractory differential hypoxemia is VAV. Make the case for axillary return instead, then argue against yourself.

If the right radial gas is fine but troponin is climbing on VA ECMO with a recovering LV, is that a coronary hypoxemia problem, a demand problem, or an unrelated graft or stent problem? How would you tell, and what would change management?

An Impella is proposed for LV unloading on day 2 in a VA ECMO patient with bad lungs. Where does differential hypoxemia sit in that risk-benefit conversation, and what monitoring would you require before agreeing?

reviewChecklist: Stage 1 vignette: cannula configuration, inotrope status, ventilator description, and pulse oximetry values are synthetic and marked [REVIEW]. Confirm they are internally consistent with NMH practice.
Stage 1 model answer: the statement that ELSO recommends right radial arterial access on peripheral VA ECMO. Confirm against the Lorusso 2021 ELSO guideline text.
Stage 1 model answer: bilateral cerebral NIRS as standard monitoring. Supported by Rosenberg 2025 but confirm you agree with how it is framed (trend, not threshold).
Stage 1 SBA explanation: the claim that modeling shows coronary hypoxia precedes cerebral hypoxia. Confirm the Stevens (or correct author) 2021 paper says this.
Stage 2 blood gas and NIRS values are invented. Confirm the right radial PaO2 of 52 on FiO2 0.5 and post-oxygenator PaO2 above 400 are the illustrative numbers you want.

Stage 3 SBA: the claim that ECPELLA can worsen differential hypoxemia. Rosenberg 2025 describes North-South physiology in ECPELLA. Confirm you endorse the mechanistic framing and whether you want it softened.
Stage 3 SBA explanation and controversies: the management sequence (lungs, then VAV, then proximal arterial return). Insert NMH's actual escalation pathway where marked.
Stage 3 model answer: VAV configuration description (IJ return cannula, Y-connector, restrictor, per-limb flow probes). Confirm this matches NMH equipment and perfusion practice.
Stage 3 model answer: anticoagulation targets and flow split left as [NMH protocol, insert].
Stage 4: the complication narrative and interpretation are expert reasoning, not guideline. Mark as such or edit.
Controversies section: all four items are stated as unsettled. Confirm you agree and that no item is actually settled at NMH.
References marked VERIFY: Lorusso 2021, Stevens 2021 (author list uncertain), Hoeper 2014, Combes 2020, Rao 2018. Confirm each exists with the stated details before release.
No numeric thresholds for saturation, NIRS, flow, or anticoagulation were asserted as recommendations. If you add any, source them.
